fact.text: Each lander had two 360-degree cylindrical scan cameras mounted near one long side of its base.
The sampler arm had a collector head, a temperature sensor and a magnet. On 28 July 1976 Viking 1's arm scooped up its first soil samples for its biology laboratory.

The landers ran three biology experiments (Labeled Release, Gas Exchange and Pyrolytic Release). They found enigmatic chemical activity in the soil, but no definitive evidence of living microorganisms.

Viking showed that the Martian surface is an iron-rich clay containing a highly oxidizing substance that releases oxygen when wetted. No organic molecules were detected at the parts-per-billion level.
A meteorology boom on one lander leg held temperature, wind direction and wind velocity sensors.
Each lander was a six-sided aluminium base on three legs. Two radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) containing plutonium-238 gave it power.
At 6 km a 16-metre parachute slowed the lander to 60 m/s. Then the aeroshell was dropped, the three legs came out, and three hydrazine engines made the final descent.
Pancam was two cameras that took detailed, multi-wavelength, 3-D panoramic pictures. Its mast stands 1.4 m tall, giving the cameras a human geologist's point of view.
The Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT) used rotating, grinding teeth to remove dust and weathered rock, exposing fresh rock underneath for the other tools.
The Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometer (APXS) found which elements make up rocks and soils, with clues to weathering and water activity on Mars.
The Mössbauer Spectrometer identified iron-bearing minerals, giving information about early Martian environmental conditions. One measurement took about 12 hours.
The Microscopic Imager, on the turret at the end of the arm, took extreme close-up black-and-white views of rocks and soils.
The rovers were solar-powered. Opportunity last communicated with Earth on 10 June 2018, as a planet-wide dust storm blanketed its location.
SEIS, the dome-shaped seismometer, sat on the Martian surface under a domed Wind and Thermal Shield and waited for marsquakes and meteorite impacts.
HP3, the heat probe, was designed to burrow almost 5 m down. Its mole met different soil than expected and could not reach the planned depth.
RISE tracked the lander's position precisely to measure how much Mars' north pole wobbles, revealing the size and composition of its iron-rich core.
After landing, the lander's arm picked up the instruments and placed them on the surface of Mars.
Ingenuity's rotors are about 1.2 m tip to tip. It could fly up to 5 m high and 300 m far in the thin Martian air.
A solar panel charged lithium-ion batteries, giving enough energy for one 90-second flight per Martian day.
Ingenuity has a mass of 1.8 kg. Planned for no more than five test flights, it completed 72 flights; the last was on 18 January 2024.
The descent engine was a deep-throttling rocket with a maximum thrust of about 45,000 N, mounted in the centre of the descent stage.
Four landing legs with round footpads held the descent stage 1.5 m above the surface; opposite footpads were 9.4 m apart.
One of the legs had a small astronaut egress platform and ladder.
The ascent stage housed the astronauts in a 6.65 cubic metre cabin with two triangular windows and no seats.
Telemetry, TV, voice and range communications with Earth all went through the steerable S-band antenna.
A parabolic rendezvous radar antenna on top helped the ascent stage find and dock with the Command and Service Module.
Four thruster modules, each with four 450 N thrusters pointing in different directions, steered the Lunar Module.
Pioneer 10 talked to Earth by radio. By the time it reached Jupiter, a command and its reply took up to 92 minutes.
Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to use all-nuclear electrical power: SNAP-19 RTGs delivering about 140 W at Jupiter.
Pioneer 10 carried a Helium Vector Magnetometer. The spacecraft's data showed that Jupiter's magnetic tail, almost 800 million km long, stretched all the way to Saturn's orbit.
The Imaging Photopolarimeter took about 500 pictures of Jupiter, showing the Great Red Spot, before Jupiter's radiation stopped it.
Pioneer 10 carries an aluminium plaque with a man and a woman, the solar system, and its location relative to 14 pulsars.
